body.text: Russia continues to grow bolder in the Western Pacific, and Australia and its partners should prepare for the implications.

On 17 November, two Russian bombers carried out an East Asian excursion in which they entered the South Korean air defence identification zone (ADIZ), violated Japanese territorial airspace, and entered the Taiwanese ADIZ for the first time since 2010. This took place just days before a historic meeting between presidents Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, sending a message that Russia was willing to flex its military muscle in support of the Sino-Russian partnership in the Pacific. This and other recent aggressive regional signalling from Moscow are reminders that Russia’s participation in a war over Taiwan is plausible and that Russian grey-zone activity in the Indo-Pacific is a growing threat.

The two Russian aircraft – likely two Tu-95MS (Bear) nuclear-capable bombers – were very likely the same two that landed that same day at Da Nang in Vietnam for Russia’s first public bomber visit since 1993. Russia is Vietnam’s biggest arms supplier, so the visit appears to be part of its message that it can poke US-aligned countries in the eye and still hold sway with significant regional players.

The flight shouldn’t be viewed in isolation. Aggressive Russian aerial activity around Japan, including breaches of its territorial airspace, has grown increasingly common in recent years. There was also nothing new in the traversing of the South Korean ADIZ – a zone, mostly in international airspace, where a country requires approaching aircraft to report themselves. However, this was only the second time Russian military aircraft are known to have entered the Taiwanese ADIZ since the fall of the Soviet Union. Doing so isn’t needed to fly from Russia to Southeast Asia.
This latest outing is therefore an escalation of previous trends, suggesting that Russia’s willingness to flex its muscle in the Indo-Pacific in ways congenial to China is growing.

While some have rightly pointed out the limits of the Sino-Russian partnership through their lack of cooperation in the Middle East and Venezuela, this incident suggests that the partnership can stand firm on major strategic issues in the Indo-Pacific. This is likely the message that Putin wished to send to Trump prior to their three-way meeting with Xi in Shenzhen: when it comes to the Pacific, Russia stands ready to assist China and supports its ambitions to dislodge the US-led order.

In December 2025, Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov said that in a potential conflict over Taiwan Russia would provide China ‘support in matters of protecting state unity and territorial integrity’. When viewed alongside Moscow’s recent aggressive activities in the region – including more regular and complex combined exercises with China – Australia and its partners should prepare for Russia’s inimical activity in the Pacific to continue to expand in scope.

At the maximalist end, this could take the form of outright Russian military support for Beijing in a Taiwan contingency. Russia could use its Pacific Fleet, and in particular its sizeable submarine arm, to create asymmetric military dilemmas for Japan and the US forces stationed there, as outlined in my recent ASPI explainer. Such a scenario would increase in likelihood if Russia coordinated an attack on a NATO country with a Chinese attack on Taiwan, meaning Russia would likely be at war with the United States anyway.

On the other hand, Russia could engage in so-called grey zone activities in the Indo-Pacific – provocative acts below the threshold of war. Russia is arguably already doing this by violating Japanese territorial airspace, but this behaviour could expand. In August 2026, Putin implied that the Pacific Fleet stood ready to seize European countries’ commercial vessels in Asia in response to their interdiction of Russia’s shadow fleet. While this hasn’t happened yet, Russia’s increasingly assertive posture suggests that this threat should be taken seriously – and perhaps being taken seriously is the goal in and of itself.

There have been multiple reports of Russia cutting submarine cables in the Baltic, so it’s not unreasonable to expect that it could undertake similar activities in the Indo-Pacific. All of these activities would help China and could shape the region to be more congenial to Sino-Russian interests. As Russia grows more aggressive in the Indo-Pacific, such moves become more likely.

This 17 November flight suggests that Russia’s actions in the Indo-Pacific are growing increasingly assertive and aligned with China’s ambitions. Given this, Australia and its partners should prepare for plausible contingencies before they materialise.
